doc.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022

title: Jazz demands listening; dance roots and poetry
summary: Jazz requires listeners to be in the music, lost its dance roots; poetry also demands quiet attention.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Do you feel that that might be one reason why jazz requires more of listeners than most pop music?

Well yes. First of all jazz does require, it has always demanded that you be in the music. Some of that has to do with dance roots and it’s unfortunate I think that jazz lost its dance roots as most of the great — as many of the great musics have done. I mean like Latin music, it retained its Latin jazz dance base but you lose a lot when you remove that dance element from it. You lose, first of all, a basic way of communicating with the audience because it’s one thing to have the music get you up out of your seat and move you, and another to have you sitting there and concentrating, which is not — which is beyond the capacity of a lot of people. A lot of people really can’t sit and be quiet and listen to music and do nothing else, just concentrate and listen for an hour or two without saying a word. So I think that — but the thing is if you can do that, you can do that, great music can do so much more for you. You know it can do a lot for you. It can inspire, it can confirm, it
can actually give direction, it can take you places you haven’t been. And so yeah, I think that the question was originally about poetry was it not?
It was. We did an improvisation.

Okay I’m trying to be like Art Tatum here, and get way, way, way off the harmonic structure of the song and find these elaborate ways to get back to it. I’m trying to do that but I am not Art Tatum. But anyway to poetry, poetry is almost antithetical to jazz in a way, especially if you write contemplative poetry as I do. I am not a performance poet. And I think the poems read well because they are basically conversational, but I don’t write for performances, a lot of contemporary poets do. There’s a generational difference. But at any rate, poetry does require of you complete attention, quietness, and a kind of subjective study, a study of the word that does not necessarily involve your reason or necessarily involve specific application to the rest of the world. It involves a different kind of application to the world. It requires a certain kind of insight that you can apply but it is not giving you specific insight in that sense of William Carlos Williams’ famous poem about how poetry — how you cannot learn the news from reading a poem but yet men die every day from lack of it. So yes, I think that poetry, and it’s basic what we used to call mind expansion back in the day, that poetry and music both offer. Poetry and serious music both offer. Your mind can expand and it can find places to settle that it would not be able to settle if you were not led there by an artist.
